subject: Accounting
title: Blockchain and Audit Trails
description: A micro-lesson that makes Blockchain and Audit Trails usable.

hook.text: What if every transaction was permanently recorded on a ledger that nobody could alter?

buildup.text: Blockchain creates an immutable, time-stamped record of every transaction in a shared ledger.

discovery.text: In theory, auditors could verify transactions instantly by reading the blockchain—no sampling needed.

twist.text: In practice, most companies don't use blockchain for accounting. Adoption is years away.

climax.text: If blockchain matures, it could make some traditional audit procedures obsolete.

punchline.text: Immutable records could make trust automatic, not audited.

details.summary: Blockchain creates immutable, timestamped records of transactions that could fundamentally change auditing by providing tamper-proof audit trails, potentially enabling continuous verification and reducing the need for third-party confirmations.
details.whyItMatters: If widely adopted, blockchain could make parts of traditional auditing obsolete by providing inherently trustworthy records that don't require independent verification by auditors.
takeaways: Blockchain records are immutable — once written, they cannot be altered or deleted
This creates a natural audit trail that is inherently more reliable than traditional records
Widespread blockchain adoption could reduce or eliminate the need for certain audit procedures

faq.question: How could blockchain change auditing?
faq.answer: Blockchain creates tamper-proof transaction records that don't need independent verification. If a company and its suppliers both record transactions on a shared blockchain, auditors wouldn't need to send confirmation letters or worry about altered records. The technology itself provides assurance.

faq.question: Is blockchain already being used in auditing?
faq.answer: Adoption is still early. Some companies use blockchain for supply chain verification and inter-company transactions. The Big Four are experimenting with blockchain tools. Full integration remains limited by adoption rates — blockchain only helps when enough parties use it.
